title: The SAD Episode
summary: Josh and Chuck open the new year with holiday banter, then explore seasonal affective disorder (SAD): its clinical classification, symptoms (winter and rarer summer patterns), risk factors (latitude, sex, genetics, existing mood disorders), the serotonin and melatonin mechanisms, treatments (SSRIs, CBT, bright light therapy, dawn simulation), and the contested status of SAD in scientific literature, including Tromsø, Norway. The episode closes with a listener email about kids playing with dolls.
topics: major depressive disorder with seasonal pattern

entities.name: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders

segments.title: New year banter and holiday recap
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck catch up on New Year's Day recording, Chuck's Broadway trip and Radio City Christmas show, and Josh's cold over the holidays.

segments.title: Introduction to SAD and its classification
segments.summary: The hosts introduce seasonal affective disorder as a real depressive disorder, not the winter blues. They cover its DSM classification, the 1984 NIH paper by Norman Rosenthal, prevalence estimates, and the summer variant. They also discuss risk factors such as sex, age, existing mood disorders, and latitude, and a Seattle ranking.

segments.title: Symptoms and when to see a doctor
segments.summary: The hosts list winter SAD symptoms such as oversleeping, carb cravings, and weight gain, and contrast them with the opposite summer symptoms. They describe the feedback loop of depression, four warning signs for seeing a professional, the two-year diagnostic guideline, and the diagnostic process.

segments.title: Evolutionary origins, sleep, and appetite
segments.summary: The hosts discuss hibernation-like winter slowdown theories, including Neanderthal interbreeding, a 2015 study of the Tsimane and San people sleeping longer in winter, a 2023 German study on sleep cycles, and seasonal appetite changes. They also cover seasonality of suicide, which peaks in spring and summer rather than during the holidays.

segments.title: Latitude and daylight study
segments.summary: The hosts cite a 2025 South Korean meta-analysis of 24 studies with about 30,000 participants, finding SAD rises with latitude. They mention the Jimmy Buffett song reference.

segments.title: Serotonin and the serotonin transporter
segments.summary: The hosts explain how reduced sunlight on the retina lowers serotonin in winter. In people with SAD, serotonin transporter activity does not drop in step, leaving less free serotonin. They also discuss estrogen's role in sex differences and the genetic short allele of the serotonin transporter gene promoter.

segments.title: Melatonin, circadian rhythm, and the SCN
segments.summary: The hosts explain melatonin's role in sleepiness and lethargy, the circadian rhythm controlled by the suprachiasmatic nucleus, the role of light as a zeitgeber, cortisol, and the finding that retinas respond less to light in winter. They also introduce social and environmental factors such as dread of winter.

segments.title: Treatments: SSRIs, CBT, and bright light therapy
segments.summary: The hosts discuss SSRI antidepressants, including seasonal ramp-up and taper, and cognitive behavioral therapy. They cover bright light therapy, including its history back to Vincenzo Chiarugi, light visors, UV protection, and library light box rentals in Northern Ireland. They also discuss dawn simulation alarm clocks.

segments.title: Vitamin D and personal anecdotes on waking
segments.summary: The hosts mention vitamin D deficiency being correlated with SAD, though supplement evidence is weak. Chuck and Josh swap alarm clock memories and sleep habits.

segments.title: Tromsø and skepticism about SAD
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Tromsø, Norway, where long winter darkness is not linked to high SAD rates, and attribute this partly to attitudes and winter traditions. They describe a 2016 study from Auburn University Montgomery finding no seasonal variation in depression using CDC data. They note that major health sites still recognize SAD and that a Scientific American link was missing.

segments.title: Danish true crime recommendation
segments.summary: Josh recommends the Danish series The Investigation, and Chuck praises Scandinavian film.

segments.title: Listener mail: Megan from Michigan on kids and dolls
segments.summary: A listener from Michigan writes that her children acted out disturbing-seeming scenarios with dolls, including funerals, and that she learned it was normal play.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh invites listeners to send in stories about their kids, and the show credits iHeartRadio.
